1212.title: Margaret Fuller
1212.hook: Fuller, editor and thinker, argued that a woman's mind deserved every path a man's had
1212.howItsDone: Readers who follow the Concord thinkers often read Margaret Fuller alongside Emerson, especially Woman in the Nineteenth Century, and some reading groups still borrow her Conversation style of posing a question and asking everyone to answer it aloud.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was the Concord circle: friends who walked, argued and read each other's drafts. Your line was a circle of friends.

A Boston parlor. A group of women sits in a ring of chairs. The woman leading them asks a big question, the kind usually saved for lecture halls. Then, instead of answering it, she waits. She wants them to answer, out loud, in their own words, and then to defend those words. These meetings were called Conversations, and the woman asking was Margaret Fuller. By Emerson's own later account, he wasn't sure about her at first. Then she became a friend he argued with in earnest, and for a time she edited the magazine the whole circle wrote for.
screen: `A RING OF CHAIRS.` → `SHE WAITS FOR THEIR ANSWERS.` → `MARGARET FULLER.`

segments.voice: First, her book, Woman in the Nineteenth Century. Its central demand is plain: every arbitrary barrier thrown down, and every path opened to women as freely as to men. Not some paths. Every path. Second, what she was not asking. She didn't want women to become copies of men. Her hope was that a woman could grow as her own nature, unfold her own mind, and live freely as a soul. The goal wasn't sameness. It was room. Third, put her next to her friend. Emerson had been telling his readers to trust thyself. Fuller asked the question underneath: trust thyself is wonderful advice, if you're allowed to have a self in public. If you're allowed to speak in the meeting, study the book, take the job, sign your own name. She took Emerson's idea of the soul seriously enough to ask who it had been left out for. Fourth, the spiritual root. Across this whole block, Emerson has said that the divine shows up in each person's own mind. Fuller drew the plain conclusion: then a mind is a mind. Nobody gets a smaller portion of the light because of who they are. That's why her Conversations mattered. She wasn't handing women answers. She was treating their thinking as worth hearing, by asking them to do it out loud.

1213.title: Against slavery
1213.hook: slow at first, Emerson came to speak strongly against slavery
1213.howItsDone: Readers of Emerson often study his later antislavery speeches alongside his early caution, as a case of a private conviction becoming public action.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Margaret Fuller, who asked that every path be opened to women. Your line was equal minds.

An honest thing to say about a man this path has spent weeks with: on the great moral wound of his country, Emerson was slow. He believed slavery was wrong, and said so in his journals. But for a long stretch he kept mostly to his study and his lectures, wary of crowds and causes and movements. Others moved sooner. By the usual account, his own wife was involved in antislavery work in Concord before he was. And people who had escaped slavery were already speaking out, at a risk he never faced. Then something changed, and the quiet man in the study stood up.
screen: `HE BELIEVED IT WAS WRONG.` → `HE STAYED IN THE STUDY.` → `THEN HE STOOD UP.`

segments.voice: First, his reasons for waiting. Emerson distrusted joining things. Self-reliance, for him, meant reforming your own soul before reforming the world, and he worried causes could swallow a person whole. There's something real in that worry. There's also something convenient in it, and later readers have said so plainly. Second, what changed. His country passed the Fugitive Slave Law, which required people in free states to help return those who had escaped slavery. Now the wrong wasn't happening somewhere else. It reached into Concord and asked him to cooperate. In his journal he wrote, in effect, that he would not obey it. Third, what he did. He began speaking in public, and sharply. He turned against Daniel Webster, a statesman he had long admired, for supporting the law. He spoke for the cause, and he welcomed the abolitionist John Brown to Concord. Whatever one thinks of every choice he made, the careful man had stopped being careful. Fourth, what it shows. A good person can hold the right belief for years and still keep it indoors. Agreeing silently felt like enough, until something made it impossible. Speaking up isn't being loud about everything. It's the moment a private conviction walks out of the study, into a room where it might cost you something.

1214.title: The house fire
1214.hook: late in life his house burned, and neighbors rebuilt it while he traveled
1214.howItsDone: In Concord the story of the Emerson house fire is told as a picture of community: neighbors saving his papers, friends paying to rebuild, and the town welcoming him home.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was against slavery: the careful man who finally left his study and spoke. Your line was speak up.

Early morning in Concord, and there's smoke coming from the Emerson house. Neighbors come running, carrying armfuls of books and papers onto the lawn: the manuscripts, the journals, years of a writer's life laid out in the grass. The roof is badly damaged. The man who wrote Self-Reliance is old now, shaken, and suddenly without a home. What happens next is the part Concord tells and retells. It isn't about Emerson trusting himself. It's about a whole town deciding not to let him stand alone.
screen: `SMOKE AT THE EMERSON HOUSE.` → `PAPERS ON THE LAWN.` → `A TOWN DECIDES.`

segments.voice: First, the rescue. By the usual account, it was neighbors who carried out his books and papers while the house burned. Whatever else was lost, a great deal of his writing survived because other people's arms got it out. Second, the gift. Friends and neighbors gathered money to rebuild the house. They urged Emerson, worn out and unwell, to go away and rest while the work was done. So he traveled abroad, and while he was gone, the town rebuilt his home. Third, the return. The story goes that when he came back, Concord met him at the station and walked him home, with bells and children and cheering, to a house standing again where the ruin had been. People who tell it say he was deeply moved. Fourth, the turn it gives this block. For weeks this path has followed Emerson's great theme: stand on your own, trust thyself. He meant it, and he lived much of it. But the self-reliant man could not rebuild his own roof. His neighbors did. Read this way, self-trust is a way of thinking, not a plan for living alone. The town didn't argue with his philosophy. It quietly added the other half: we rely on each other, too. Some traditions call that charity, some call it community, some call it being a neighbor. Concord simply got to work.

1215.title: Emerson forgetting
1215.hook: in old age Emerson's memory faded; he forgot words but kept his gentleness
1215.howItsDone: Readers of Emerson often end with his late poem Terminus and the accounts of his final years, when his memory faded and those near him remembered his gentleness.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was the house fire: a town rebuilt the roof the self-reliant man couldn't. Your line was neighbors rebuild.

A story people tell about Emerson in his last years. He wants to ask for his umbrella, and the word won't come. So he describes it instead: the thing that strangers take away. A man who spent his life finding exactly the right word, reaching for an everyday one and missing it, and landing on something oddly lovely anyway. In his old age, Emerson's memory faded. Names slipped, then words. In time the lectures and the writing fell away. And yet the people around him kept telling one more thing about those years.
screen: `THE WORD WON'T COME.` → `THE THING STRANGERS TAKE AWAY.` → `NAMES, THEN WORDS.`

segments.voice: First, he saw it coming. Some years before the fading, Emerson wrote a poem called Terminus, a word for a boundary stone. It opens, "It is time to be old," and speaks of taking in sail, like a ship coming into harbor. It isn't a bitter poem. It reads like a man setting his affairs in order and choosing to be at peace with the tide. Second, the forgetting itself. Another story people tell: at the funeral of a dear friend, the poet Longfellow, Emerson looked at the face for a long time and said, in effect, that he couldn't remember the name, but this had been a sweet and beautiful soul. The name was gone. The love wasn't. Third, what stayed. Those who cared for him, his daughter Ellen among them, described a man still courteous, still smiling, still kind to visitors he could no longer place. The words had gone; the manner remained. Fourth, why it matters here. This path has spent weeks with Emerson's mind. His last years ask a quieter question: if the mind goes, what's left? In his case, the answer people remembered was gentleness. Some traditions say, in their own way, that who a person is runs deeper than what a person remembers. However you understand that, the old man forgetting the name and keeping the love is hard to forget.

1216.title: Days, the poem
1216.hook: in his poem Days, the days pass like silent gift-bearers and he takes only a few herbs
1216.howItsDone: Days is a short poem often read aloud or memorized by readers of Emerson, as a reminder to notice what each ordinary day offers.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Emerson forgetting: the name gone, the gentleness still there. Your line was gentleness stays.

A procession goes past a garden, single file, no end to it. The walkers are barefoot and silent, wrapped so you can't see their faces. Each one carries something: some carry crowns, some bundles of sticks for the fire. Each stops in front of whoever is watching and offers a gift, whatever that person wants. A man sits in his garden and watches them go by. One stops in front of him. That's the scene of a short poem Emerson called Days. The walkers are the days themselves, and what the man picks is the reason the poem stings.
screen: `A SILENT PROCESSION.` → `EACH ONE OFFERS A GIFT.` → `THE WALKERS ARE THE DAYS.`

segments.voice: First, the disguise. The poem opens, "Daughters of Time, the hypocritic Days." Hypocritic is an odd word for a day. Emerson means they wear a mask. A day looks plain, one more Tuesday, and hides what it's carrying. Second, the offer: "To each they offer gifts after his will, Bread, kingdoms, stars, and sky that holds them all." Bread at one end, the whole sky at the other. Each day, the poem says, offers whatever you're willing to ask for, from the smallest need to the largest wonder. Third, what he took. The man forgets what he wished for that morning. He reaches out, and he "Took a few herbs and apples, and the Day Turned and departed silent." Not wrong, not wicked, just small: less than was offered, out of hurry or habit. Then, too late, the poem says, he saw the Day's scorn under her solemn headband. Fourth, what's new here. Earlier on this path, in an essay, Emerson pictured the days as veiled figures bearing gifts. In the poem, the blame turns on the watcher: he forgot his morning wishes. It isn't a poem about doing more. Herbs and apples are good things. It's about noticing what's being held out, and asking for something real: a conversation instead of a scroll, an hour outside instead of one more errand.

segments.voice: Go back to the start of your own day, or the last quiet moment you had, and look for a wish in it: to call someone, to be outside for an hour, to make something, or to rest. Let one forgotten wish come back. Then ask what today could hand you toward it, if you asked for more than herbs.

1217.title: Emerson's limits
1217.hook: critics say his optimism skips over evil and suffering
1217.howItsDone: Readers and teachers of Emerson often pair his hopeful essays with the criticism that they pass too lightly over evil and suffering, and with his own writing on grief and limits.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Days: masked walkers holding out bread and sky, and a man who took a few herbs. Your line was the days bring gifts.

Read enough Emerson in one sitting and a question starts to press. The stars are a revelation. Every act rewards or punishes itself. Trust thyself and the universe will meet you. Nothing can bring you peace but yourself. It's bracing. It's lovely. Then you put the book down and turn on the news, or sit in a hospital waiting room, or remember what was happening in his own country while he wrote. Where, in all that light, is the dark? Readers have asked that about Emerson for a long time. Today, the case against him, told fairly, and what's still standing after it.
screen: `ALL THAT LIGHT.` → `THE HOSPITAL WAITING ROOM.` → `WHERE IS THE DARK?`

segments.voice: First, the charge. Some critics, in his time and since, say Emerson's optimism skips over evil. His essay Compensation says every act comes back to its doer, but innocent people suffer for things they never did. The Over-Soul holds every life in something larger, but that can sound distant to someone in pain. And a philosophy built on self-trust has little to say to someone whose self has been broken by illness or cruelty. Second, his own country. Emerson wrote his brightest pages while slavery was the law in much of it, and, as this path saw a few days ago, he was slow to speak. Critics ask whether a sunny view of the soul made it easier to look away. Third, the defense, and it's real. Emerson knew grief. He lost his young wife, brothers he loved, and his little son, after whose death he wrote that grief could teach him nothing. That's not the sentence of a man who never looked into the dark. Later essays face limits head on, the things a person cannot will away. His hope wasn't naive so much as stubborn. Fourth, the useful middle. Both can be true. His hope is a real gift, and it has edges where it stops working. Carry it the way a hiker carries a good map that doesn't show every cliff: use it, love it, know where it ends. Hope with limits isn't weaker hope. It's hope that has been honest about the waiting room.

1218.title: What to keep from Emerson
1218.hook: self-trust, nature, the sacred in the ordinary
1218.howItsDone: Readers who spend time with Emerson often name a few ideas they carry away, such as self-trust, the renewing power of nature, and the holiness of ordinary life.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Emerson's limits: a real hope, with edges where it stops working. Your line was hope with limits.

A week ends today, and so, almost, does this long walk with Emerson. This week held Margaret Fuller asking who gets to think, the careful man finally speaking against slavery, a town rebuilding his roof, the old man forgetting names and keeping his gentleness, the masked days holding out their gifts, and yesterday, the fair case against him. Emerson wouldn't want to be carried around whole. He warned scholars not to let any book, even a great one, do their thinking for them. So today is a packing question, the kind you ask at the end of a long trip with a small bag: what's worth carrying home?
screen: `A WEEK ENDS.` → `DON'T CARRY HIM WHOLE.` → `A SMALL BAG.`

segments.voice: Here are three things some readers keep. First, self-trust. Not selfishness, as this path saw when it read Self-Reliance carefully, but the courage to look with your own eyes. Emerson's point was that the same light that spoke to the great teachers can speak to you, and that copying someone else's insight is never quite the same as having your own. Second, nature. In his first book, Nature, he wrote that in the woods a person returns to reason and faith. Some readers still keep that: a walk as a kind of prayer or a kind of clearing, whatever word fits their own path. Third, the sacred in the ordinary. Some find this one the deepest. In The American Scholar he wrote, "I embrace the common, I explore and sit at the feet of the familiar, the low." The kitchen, the street, the farm, the walk to work. The holy wasn't hiding far away; it was in plain sight, wearing the mask of an ordinary day, as his poem Days put it. And the honest fourth: whatever you keep, keep it with yesterday's limits attached. Self-trust beside the neighbors who rebuild. Nature beside the waiting room. The sacred ordinary beside the people for whom ordinary life is hard. The point isn't to keep everything. In his spirit, the advice might be: keep one, and make it yours.
screen: `SELF-TRUST: LOOK WITH YOUR OWN EYES.` · `NATURE: BACK TO THE WOODS.` · `THE SACRED IN THE ORDINARY.` · `KEEP IT WITH ITS LIMITS.` · then, large: `KEEP ONE.`

segments.voice: Lay the three out like objects on a table, self-trust, nature, the sacred in the ordinary, and look at each for a breath or two. Notice which one your hand moves toward, and pick it up without arguing. Then think of one place in your actual week where it could live: a decision, a walk, a sink full of dishes.
What to keep from Emerson. Self-trust, nature, and the sacred in the ordinary, each carried with its limits, and the advice to keep one and make it yours. Today's word.
